result.summary: This short section gives two fragments attributed to a lost Hesiodic poem, the Great Works. The first is a saying about reaping what one sows, tied to the slaying of Rhadamanthys. The second is a note that Hesiod there links silver with Earth.

scenes.title: Two fragments of the Great Works
scenes.summary: Ancient commentators quote or report two passages from the Great Works: a maxim of retributive justice, and a claim that silver belongs to Earth's family.

characters.name: Hesiod
characters.description: Archaic Greek poet to whom the Great Works is attributed

characters.name: Rhadamanthys
characters.description: Figure whose slaying is linked to the quoted verse

characters.name: Earth
characters.description: Primal goddess whose family silver is said to belong to

notable_quotes.reason: A memorable statement of retributive justice: those who sow evil reap evil.

analysis.text: The first fragment expresses reciprocal justice, that harm returns to the doer. This idea fits the moral outlook of Hesiod's Works and Days.
Both fragments survive only because later commentators, Aristotle's and Proclus's, quoted them. This shows how much early Greek poetry is known only second-hand.

fun_facts.text: The Great Works is lost, and ancient writers sometimes treated it as a separate poem from the Works and Days.

language_notes.text: Rhadamanthys, a son of Zeus and Europa, was a judge in the afterlife in some traditions. The 'verse' about his slaying of justice is cited to illustrate retribution (the 'Rhadamanthine' principle).
'Reap evil increase' means harvest a growing yield of evil; 'increase' is an old word for crop or produce.
'Of the family of Earth' means descended from or akin to Gaia, so silver would be an offspring of the earth itself.
The Silver Race is the second human age in Hesiod's Works and Days; some ancients linked it to earth via the metal's origin.

context_notes.text: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics book 5 discusses reciprocal justice; commentators cited Hesiod to illustrate the idea of suffering what one has done.
Proclus was a late ancient Neoplatonist who wrote a commentary on Hesiod's Works and Days, preserving fragments from lost poems.

literary_notes.text: Sowing and reaping stand for deeds and their consequences, presenting wrongdoing as a crop that returns multiplied to the doer.
Earth is treated as a parent with a family, so a metal becomes her kin and offspring.
